topics.title: Mass - kg and g: Compare objects using kilograms and grams; measure using scales

questions.stem: A classroom calculator has a mass of 100 grams. An equal-arm balance is used to balance the calculator with Base 10 longs (10 g each), marbles (5 g each), and chalk sticks (2 g each). How many of each unit are needed to balance the calculator?

options: Base 10 longs, because every Base 10 long has the exact same uniform mass and flat shape, whereas marbles can vary in size and chalk sticks wear down or break
Chalk sticks, because broken pieces of chalk of different lengths are the most accurate way to measure mass
Marbles, because round glass balls roll off surfaces easily and come in many different sizes
None of them, because an equal-arm balance can only compare length and not mass

steps.explain: A good informal measuring unit for mass must be **uniform** (every piece has the exact same mass) and easy to stack in the balance pan without rolling or breaking.
steps.work: \(\text{Best unit} = \text{Uniform mass and easy to handle}\)

questions.stem: Match each grocery item to its most sensible mass: a can of baked beans, a packet of sugar, a large bag of potatoes, and a 2 L bottle of milk.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 100" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:429px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="332" height="92" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170" y="38" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Items: Baked beans, Sugar, Potatoes, 2 L Milk</text><text x="170" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#0369a1">Masses: 1/2 kg,   1 kg,   2 kg,   5 kg</text></svg>

options: Baked beans: 1/2 kg, Sugar: 1 kg, Milk: 2 kg, Potatoes: 5 kg
Baked beans: 5 kg, Sugar: 2 kg, Milk: 1 kg, Potatoes: 1/2 kg
Baked beans: 1 kg, Sugar: 1/2 kg, Milk: 5 kg, Potatoes: 2 kg
Baked beans: 2 kg, Sugar: 5 kg, Milk: 1/2 kg, Potatoes: 1 kg

steps.explain: Recall that 1 L of water/milk has a mass of about 1 kg, so a 2 L bottle of milk has a mass of 2 kg.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:429px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="332" height="88" rx="10" fill="#fef9c3" stroke="#ca8a04" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#854d0e">2 L Milk = 2 kg   |   Standard Sugar = 1 kg</text></svg>

steps.explain: A small tin of baked beans is about half a kilogram (500 g = 1/2 kg), a packet of sugar is 1 kg, and a large bag of potatoes is the heaviest at 5 kg.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:429px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="332" height="88" rx="10" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">Beans 1/2 kg < Sugar 1 kg < Milk 2 kg < Potatoes 5 kg</text></svg>

steps.explain: Order from lightest to heaviest: baked beans (1/2 kg) < sugar (1 kg) < 2 L milk (2 kg) < potatoes (5 kg).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:429px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="332" height="88" rx="10" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">Beans 1/2 kg < Sugar 1 kg < Milk 2 kg < Potatoes 5 kg</text></svg>

steps.explain: Therefore, Baked beans: 1/2 kg, Sugar: 1 kg, Milk: 2 kg, Potatoes: 5 kg is correct.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:429px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="332" height="88" rx="10" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="170" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">Beans 1/2 kg < Sugar 1 kg < Milk 2 kg < Potatoes 5 kg</text></svg>

questions.hint: Order the four grocery items from lightest to heaviest and match them with 1/2 kg, 1 kg, 2 kg, and 5 kg.

keyPoints.note: 1 L of milk/water weighs about 1 kg.

questions.stem: One litre of water has a mass of 1 kilogram (1 kg). What is the mass of \(2\dfrac{1}{2}\) litres of water (in kg and in grams)?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:377px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="292" height="88" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#0369a1">1 L water = 1 kg = 1000 g</text><text x="150" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">2 1/2 L water = ? kg (? g)</text></svg>

steps.explain: Since 1 L of water has a mass of 1 kg, 2 L of water has a mass of 2 kg (2000 g).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:377px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="292" height="88" rx="10" fill="#fef9c3" stroke="#ca8a04" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#854d0e">2 kg (2000 g) + 1/2 kg (500 g)</text></svg>

steps.explain: Half a litre of water has a mass of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) kg = 500 g.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:377px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="292" height="88" rx="10" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">2 1/2 kg = 2500 g</text></svg>

steps.explain: Combine both parts: 2000 g + 500 g = 2500 g, or \(2\dfrac{1}{2}\) kg.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:377px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="292" height="88" rx="10" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">2 1/2 kg = 2500 g</text></svg>

steps.explain: Therefore, \(2\dfrac{1}{2}\) litres of water has a mass of \(2\dfrac{1}{2}\) kg (2500 g).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 96" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:377px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="292" height="88" rx="10" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">2 1/2 kg = 2500 g</text></svg>

questions.hint: Remember 1 L of water = 1 kg (1000 g) and half a kilogram = 500 g.

keyPoints.note: 1 L of water has a mass of 1 kg (1000 g).

questions.stem: How many 2 kg flour items can be packed into a bag that holds 24 kg?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 116" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:410px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="312" height="108" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="20" y="22" width="76" height="54" rx="8" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="58" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#92400e">Bag limit</text><text x="58" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">24 kg</text><line x1="98" y1="49" x2="144" y2="49" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="121" y="40" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">÷ 2 kg</text><rect x="148" y="24" width="68" height="50" rx="6" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="182" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="10.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Flour</text><text x="182" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#0369a1">2 kg</text><rect x="230" y="26" width="72" height="46" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="266" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#94a3b8">?</text><text x="160" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">How many 2 kg packs fit in 24 kg?</text></svg>

steps.explain: Divide the 24 kg bag limit by the mass of one flour item (2 kg): 24 ÷ 2.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 116" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:410px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="312" height="108" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="20" y="22" width="76" height="54" rx="8" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="58" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#92400e">Bag limit</text><text x="58" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">24 kg</text><line x1="98" y1="49" x2="144" y2="49" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="121" y="40" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">÷ 2 kg</text><rect x="148" y="24" width="68" height="50" rx="6" fill="#fef08a" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="182" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="10.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Flour</text><text x="182" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#0369a1">2 kg</text><rect x="230" y="26" width="72" height="46" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="266" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#94a3b8">?</text><text x="160" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">24 kg ÷ 2 kg = 12</text></svg>

steps.explain: Calculate 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 116" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:410px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="312" height="108" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="20" y="22" width="76" height="54" rx="8" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="58" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#92400e">Bag limit</text><text x="58" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">24 kg</text><line x1="98" y1="49" x2="144" y2="49" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="121" y="40" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">÷ 2 kg</text><rect x="148" y="24" width="68" height="50" rx="6" fill="#fef08a" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="182" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="10.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Flour</text><text x="182" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#0369a1">2 kg</text><rect x="230" y="26" width="72" height="46" rx="8" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="266" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">12</text><text x="160" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#15803d">24 kg ÷ 2 kg = 12</text></svg>

steps.explain: Check with multiplication: 12 × 2 kg = 24 kg.

questions.solution: Moving from \(12\) to \(2\) is \(2\) number spaces of \(5\) minutes each, which takes \(2 \times 5 = 10\) minutes.

questions.stem: The minute hand counts \(60\) minutes every hour, and each number on the clock represents a span of \(5\) minutes. In c, how many minutes does it take for the minute hand to move from \(12\) to \(3\)?

questions.solution: Moving from \(12\) to \(3\) is \(3\) number spaces of \(5\) minutes each, which takes \(3 \times 5 = 15\) minutes.

questions.stem: The minute hand counts \(60\) minutes every hour, and each number on the clock represents a span of \(5\) minutes. In e, how many minutes does it take for the minute hand to move from \(12\) to \(6\)?

questions.solution: Moving from \(12\) to \(6\) is \(6\) number spaces of \(5\) minutes each, which takes \(6 \times 5 = 30\) minutes.

questions.stem: The minute hand counts \(60\) minutes every hour, and each number on the clock represents a span of \(5\) minutes. In g, how many minutes does it take for the minute hand to move from \(4\) to \(6\)?

keyPoints.note: Count the number of steps between the two clock numbers and multiply by 5 minutes for each step.

questions.solution: Moving from \(4\) to \(6\) is \(2\) number spaces of \(5\) minutes each, which takes \(2 \times 5 = 10\) minutes.

questions.stem: The minute hand counts \(60\) minutes every hour, and each number on the clock represents a span of \(5\) minutes. In i, how many minutes does it take for the minute hand to move from \(6\) to \(9\)?

keyPoints.note: Count the number of steps between the two clock numbers and multiply by 5 minutes for each step.

questions.solution: Moving from \(6\) to \(9\) is \(3\) number spaces of \(5\) minutes each, which takes \(3 \times 5 = 15\) minutes.

keyPoints.note: Each clock number is 5 minutes. Count 5 minutes clockwise from 12.

questions.solution: To show \(5\text{ past }12\), the minute hand must be pointing to the 1 (5 minutes past 12).

steps.explain: Read the target time on watch a: \(5\text{ past }12\) means \(5\) minutes past \(12\text{ o'clock}\).

questions.hint: Start at \(12\) (\(0\) minutes) and count clockwise by \(5\)s for each clock number (and by \(1\)s for individual minute marks) to reach \(20\) minutes.

keyPoints.note: Each clock number is 5 minutes. Count 20 minutes clockwise from 12.

questions.solution: To show \(20\text{ past }12\), the minute hand must be pointing to the 4 (20 minutes past 12).

steps.explain: Read the target time on watch c: \(20\text{ past }12\) means \(20\) minutes past \(12\text{ o'clock}\).

keyPoints.note: Each clock number is 5 minutes. Count 15 minutes clockwise from 12.

questions.solution: To show \(15\text{ past }12\), the minute hand must be pointing to the 3 (15 minutes past 12).

steps.explain: Read the target time on watch e: \(15\text{ past }12\) means \(15\) minutes past \(12\text{ o'clock}\).

keyPoints.note: Each clock number is 5 minutes. Count 25 minutes clockwise from 12.

questions.solution: To show \(25\text{ past }12\), the minute hand must be pointing to the 5 (25 minutes past 12).

steps.explain: Read the target time on watch g: \(25\text{ past }12\) means \(25\) minutes past \(12\text{ o'clock}\).

keyPoints.note: The number before "past" tells how many minutes have passed since the hour.
Divide the number of minutes by 5 (or count by 5s from 12) to find which clock number the minute hand points to.

questions.stem: The clock shows the hour hand for the time "15 past 8". Which number on the clock face should the minute hand point to so the clock shows "15 past 8"?

questions.hint: Start at 12 and skip count by 5s around the clock face (1 = 5 minutes, 2 = 10 minutes, 3 = 15 minutes, and so on) until you reach the number of minutes past the hour.

keyPoints.note: The number before "past" tells how many minutes have passed since the hour.
Divide the number of minutes by 5 (or count by 5s from 12) to find which clock number the minute hand points to.

questions.stem: The clock shows the hour hand for the time "25 past 12". Which number on the clock face should the minute hand point to so the clock shows "25 past 12"?

questions.hint: Start at 12 and skip count by 5s around the clock face (1 = 5 minutes, 2 = 10 minutes, 3 = 15 minutes, and so on) until you reach the number of minutes past the hour.

keyPoints.note: The number before "past" tells how many minutes have passed since the hour.
Divide the number of minutes by 5 (or count by 5s from 12) to find which clock number the minute hand points to.

questions.stem: Look at the analogue clock face. What time does the clock show?

steps.explain: Look at the long minute hand (red): it points straight up to 12 (0 minutes).
Look at the short hour hand (orange): it points to 12.
Put the minutes and hour together to read the clock: 12 o'clock.

keyPoints.note: Short hand shows the hour; long hand shows the minutes.

questions.stem: Look at the analogue clock face. What time does the clock show?

steps.explain: Look at the long minute hand (red): it points straight down to 6 (30 minutes = half past).
Look at the short hour hand (orange): it is halfway between 1 and 2.
Put the minutes and hour together to read the clock: Half past 1.

keyPoints.note: Short hand shows the hour; long hand shows the minutes.

questions.stem: Look at the analogue clock face. What time does the clock show?

steps.explain: Look at the long minute hand (red): it points to 4 (4 × 5 = 20 minutes past).
Look at the short hour hand (orange): it is just past 4.
Put the minutes and hour together to read the clock: 20 past 4.

keyPoints.note: Short hand shows the hour; long hand shows the minutes.

questions.stem: Look at the analogue clock face. What time does the clock show?

steps.explain: Look at the long minute hand (red): it points to 10 (10 minutes to the next hour).
Look at the short hour hand (orange): it is nearly at 6.
Put the minutes and hour together to read the clock: 10 to 6.

keyPoints.note: Short hand shows the hour; long hand shows the minutes.

questions.stem: Look at the analogue clock face. What time does the clock show?

steps.explain: Look at the long minute hand (red): it points to 3 (15 minutes = quarter past).
Look at the short hour hand (orange): it is just past 7.
Put the minutes and hour together to read the clock: Quarter past 7.

questions.hint: Read the long minute hand first (3 = quarter past, 6 = half past, 9 = quarter to, or count by 5s from 12), then check the short hour hand.

keyPoints.note: Short hand shows the hour; long hand shows the minutes.

questions.stem: Look at the analogue clock face. What time does the clock show?

steps.explain: Look at the long minute hand (red): it points to 9 (15 minutes = quarter to the next hour).
Look at the short hour hand (orange): it is almost at 5.
Put the minutes and hour together to read the clock: Quarter to 5.

questions.stem: How many minutes does it take the hour hand to move from one number to the next on a clock?
questions.hint: Careful! The question asks about the hour hand, not the minute hand. Moving from one hour number to the next (for example, from \(1\) to \(2\)) is \(1\) full hour.

keyPoints.text: hour hand to move from one number to the next
keyPoints.note: The hour hand takes 1 full hour to move from one clock number to the next.

questions.solution: The hour hand moves from one number to the next in \(1\) hour, which is \(60\text{ minutes}\).

steps.explain: Read the question carefully: it asks about the hour hand (which shows hours), not the minute hand.
While the hour hand moves from one number to the next (such as from \(12\) to \(1\)), the minute hand travels all the way around the clock face once.
steps.work: \(1\text{ full turn of the minute hand} = 60\text{ minutes}\)

steps.explain: Convert \(1\) hour into minutes: \(1\text{ hour} = 60\text{ minutes}\) (whereas \(5\) minutes is for the minute hand).
Therefore, it takes the hour hand \(60\text{ minutes}\) to move from one number to the next.
